scenes.narration: This chapter tackles the single most confused pair on either exam. We're talking about R D S — Amazon's managed relational database service — and specifically two of its features that sound almost identical: Multi, A Z, and read replicas. Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby in a second availability zone purely so the database can fail over automatically if the primary dies. A read replica is a completely different thing — an asynchronous copy built to soak up extra read traffic, not to save you during an outage. This material sits inside Design Resilient Architectures, twenty six percent of the associate exam, and Design High-Performing Architectures, another twenty four percent — so getting this distinction automatic is worth a meaningful chunk of your score. We'll also widen out to when you'd reach for Aurora instead of a stock engine, and when the real answer isn't a relational database at all.

facts.label: Multi-AZ
facts.value: Synchronous standby — automatic failover, not directly readable

facts.label: Read replica
facts.value: Asynchronous copy — read scaling, promotion is manual

scenes.narration: Here's the trap almost every practice exam includes at least once. A candidate sees "survive an outage" and "handle more reads" as two versions of the same idea — add a second copy of the database — and assumes either feature can solve either problem. So they enable Multi-AZ and expect it to quietly take reporting load off the primary, or they stand up a read replica and assume it's now protected if the primary dies. There's an even subtler version one layer down: Aurora's replicas are genuinely fast and low-lag, which tempts people into assuming any AWS database "replica" must offer that same automatic failover guarantee. It doesn't — that speed is specific to Aurora's storage design, not a rule that generalizes back to stock engines.

props.heading: "They're both just extra copies of the database"
bullets: Enable Multi-AZ and expect it to also absorb reporting read traffic.
Stand up a read replica and assume it now protects against the primary failing.
Assume Aurora Replicas' low lag means any RDS "replica" auto-fails-over.

scenes.narration: Walk through why these two can't substitute for each other. Multi-AZ's replication is synchronous — every write has to reach the standby before RDS calls the transaction durable, so the standby is always caught up. That's exactly why it's safe to auto-promote it during a failure, typically within about a minute or two, with the same endpoint just repointed underneath your application. But that standby is never queryable — it's pure insurance, not extra capacity. A read replica works the opposite way: it applies changes only after the primary already committed them, so it can lag, and that lag is precisely why it's safe to route read traffic there without slowing down writes. Promoting one to standalone is a manual, deliberate, one-way operation, never an automatic response to an outage. And critically, these aren't either-or — a solid production design commonly runs Multi-AZ on the primary for failover safety and layers read replicas on top for scaling, at the same time.

props.heading: Synchronous failover vs asynchronous scaling
steps: Multi-AZ writes go to the standby synchronously — durable before commit, always caught up
RDS auto-detects a dead primary and promotes the standby, typically within 1–2 minutes
The standby is never a read target — it's insurance, not capacity
Read replicas apply changes after the primary commits — lag is normal and expected
Promoting a replica is manual and permanently breaks the replication link
They compose — Multi-AZ on the primary plus read replicas on top, at the same time

scenes.narration: Put the two side by side and the pattern is mechanical, not something you have to memorize. Replication: synchronous versus asynchronous. Purpose: automatic failover versus read scaling. Only the read replica is actually queryable — Multi-AZ's standby never is, under any configuration. Promotion: Multi-AZ promotes itself automatically in roughly a minute or two; a read replica only promotes when a human, or a script, deliberately tells it to, and that's permanent. And notice the last row — these aren't mutually exclusive. They're two separate knobs you can turn on the same database at the same time.

props.heading: Multi-AZ vs read replica, the exam's favorite trap

rows.label: Can combine?
cells: Yes — a replica can itself be Multi-AZ

scenes.narration: Aurora's real trick isn't a new query language or a different engine — it's wire-compatible with MySQL or PostgreSQL, so your application code and drivers barely notice a difference. What actually changed is underneath: a distributed, self-healing storage layer that's already replicated across multiple availability zones, decoupled entirely from the compute instances sitting on top of it. Because the writer and every reader are already pointed at that same shared storage, promoting a reader or failing over doesn't require re-copying data the way a stock engine's separate-storage-per-instance model does — that's the actual reason it's typically faster, not just a marketing number. Storage itself also auto-scales as your data grows, no manual volume provisioning, though you still choose and size your compute instances yourself. And Aurora supports up to fifteen low-lag read replicas sharing that one storage layer, more than a stock engine typically allows.

props.heading: It's the storage layer, not a new database engine
bullets: Wire-compatible with MySQL or PostgreSQL — application code and drivers barely change.
Storage is distributed, self-healing, and decoupled from compute, replicated across multiple AZs.
Shared storage means failover and replica promotion skip re-copying data — that's why they're faster.
Storage auto-scales with the data; you still size and choose compute instances yourself.
Up to 15 Aurora Replicas can share that storage with very low replication lag.

scenes.narration: This is the table that resolves most of the exam's data-layer scenario questions. If nothing forces a specific stock engine or licensing version, Aurora is usually the stronger relational default over plain RDS, because of that faster failover and auto-scaling storage. If the access pattern is fundamentally key-based lookups at large or unpredictable scale, with no real need for joins, that's DynamoDB's job — not a relational database stretched past what it's good at. And if the actual bottleneck is just repeated reads of the same hot data, ElastiCache sits in front of whichever database is the real system of record; it never replaces that database. The exam rewards matching the tool to the exact stated pattern, never reaching for whichever option merely sounds the most powerful.

props.heading: RDS vs Aurora vs DynamoDB vs ElastiCache

rows.label: RDS
cells: A hard stock-engine version or licensing constraint rules Aurora out
Nothing forces a specific engine — Aurora is usually the stronger default

rows.label: Aurora
cells: Faster failover/promotion and auto-scaling storage, up to 15 low-lag replicas
A named engine-version or compatibility constraint Aurora doesn't support

rows.label: DynamoDB
cells: Access is key-based lookups at very large or unpredictable scale
The workload needs joins or complex, ad-hoc relational queries

rows.label: ElastiCache
cells: The bottleneck is repeated reads of the same hot data
The cached data is meant to be the system of record

scenes.narration: You're never asked to write these files from memory, but you should recognize what each one implements. primary.yaml is where Multi-AZ actually lives — it's a boolean property set on the primary instance itself, not a separate resource you stand up. read-replica.yaml names its own identifier and explicitly points a source field back at the primary — a genuinely separate resource, not a setting. aurora-cluster.yaml exposes both a writer endpoint and a reader endpoint sitting on that one shared storage layer underneath. And the params folder holds the parameter groups each engine needs — a small detail, but one the exam occasionally checks you can locate.

props.kicker: THE I A C, ORGANIZED BY INTENT
props.heading: data-tier/
lines: ├── primary.yaml        # MultiAZ: true — a flag on the instance, not a resource
├── read-replica.yaml   # SourceDBInstanceIdentifier points back at primary
├── aurora-cluster.yaml # writer + reader endpoints, one shared storage layer
└── params/             # parameter groups, one set per engine

scenes.narration: Three commands map to the three mechanisms this chapter is built around. create-db-instance with the multi-az flag provisions the primary and its synchronous standby together — notice multi-az is a flag on the instance itself, not a separate resource you create afterward. create-db-instance-read-replica is a genuinely different call: it names its own identifier and points a separate source-db-instance-identifier field back at the primary, exactly the two-different-resources distinction from earlier. And promote-read-replica is the one-way door — run it during a deliberate disaster-recovery exercise, or a real incident, and the former replica becomes an independent, standalone, writable database with no path back to being a replica again.

props.heading: From a Multi-AZ primary to a promoted replica

output: Promotion started — this permanently breaks the replication link
billing-report-replica is now a standalone, writable instance

scenes.narration: Take a concrete case. Ledgerline runs its core billing database on RDS for PostgreSQL. Their real fear is losing the whole availability zone hosting the primary during month-end billing runs, when even a few minutes of downtime means missed invoices. Separately, reporting queries running straight against the primary have started causing lock contention that slows down the actual billing writes. The tempting shortcut is "just turn on Multi-AZ, that fixes resilience and takes the reporting load off too" — but the standby still isn't queryable, so it does nothing for the reporting problem. Worked through the framework properly: enable Multi-AZ for the failover requirement, and separately stand up a read replica and point reporting traffic at it. Two different problems, two different features, both genuinely needed at once.

scenes.narration: Try these yourselves before we reveal the answers. First: a team enables Multi-AZ specifically hoping it'll also soak up reporting traffic, and after deployment nothing's improved — why not? Second, and this one's sharper: a runbook says "fail over via Multi-AZ" to recover from an accidental bulk delete, and a reviewer flags it as wrong. What's actually broken about that plan?

questions.prompt: A team enables Multi-AZ on its RDS primary specifically hoping it will also absorb reporting query traffic. After deployment, reporting queries are still hitting the primary and performance hasn't improved. What's the most likely explanation?
options: Multi-AZ only takes effect after a full failover event, not before one
The Multi-AZ standby isn't directly queryable — offloading reads requires a separate read replica
Reporting queries need to be rewritten to target DynamoDB instead
Multi-AZ must be paired with ElastiCache before any reads can be offloaded

questions.prompt: A team's disaster-recovery runbook says to "fail over via Multi-AZ" to recover from an accidental bulk delete on their production database. A reviewer flags this as wrong. Why?
options: Multi-AZ failover takes too long to be useful during an active incident
The synchronous standby received the same bulk delete at essentially the same moment, so failing over recovers nothing — a point-in-time restore is needed instead
Multi-AZ can only fail over automatically, never on a manual runbook step, so this instruction can't be executed
Bulk deletes can only be reversed by promoting a read replica, never through backups

scenes.narration: Here's why. The standby is a synchronous failover target and nothing else — it was never built to serve reads, so no amount of Multi-AZ configuration changes that; only a real read replica offloads reporting traffic. And the runbook example is the sneakier trap: Multi-AZ's standby received that same accidental bulk delete synchronously, at essentially the same instant as the primary, so failing over just moves you to an equally corrupted copy. Recovering from human error needs a completely different mechanism — a point-in-time restore from an automated backup or a manual snapshot, which always creates a brand-new instance rather than rewinding the existing one in place.

answers.prompt: Why didn't Multi-AZ help reporting query performance?
answers.correct: The standby isn't directly queryable — it's a synchronous failover target only, never a read endpoint.
answers.rationale: Multi-AZ and read scaling are two different features solving two different problems. Offloading reporting reads always requires a separate read replica; enabling Multi-AZ alone never provides that, regardless of configuration.

answers.prompt: Why is "fail over via Multi-AZ" the wrong recovery step for an accidental bulk delete?
answers.correct: The standby received the same bad delete synchronously — failing over just moves the corrupted state, it doesn't undo it.
answers.rationale: Multi-AZ protects against instance and AZ failure, not against bad writes. Data corruption or human error needs a point-in-time restore from an automated backup or manual snapshot, which always creates a brand-new instance rather than fixing the existing primary or standby in place.

scenes.narration: Five things to carry forward. Multi-AZ is synchronous failover, read replicas are asynchronous read scaling, and they layer together rather than replacing each other. Aurora's real advantage is a distributed, self-healing storage layer decoupled from compute — that's the actual reason failover, replica promotion, and storage scaling are all faster or automatic, not just a marketing claim. Backups and snapshots are a completely separate mechanism, aimed at a third failure mode: data corruption or human error, not an instance or availability-zone loss. DynamoDB and ElastiCache aren't scaled-down relational databases — reach for DynamoDB when access is fundamentally key-based at large scale, and ElastiCache when the bottleneck is repeated hot reads in front of whatever the real database is. And above all, match the tool to the exact failure domain or access pattern a scenario names — never assume one mechanism quietly covers all three failure modes at once. Next up: chapter nine goes deep on the option this chapter kept deferring — DynamoDB's partition and sort keys, and the hot-partition trap that catches even experienced engineers.

props.heading: What to remember from this chapter
takeaways: Multi-AZ is synchronous failover; read replicas are asynchronous read scaling — they compose, they don't substitute.
Aurora's real edge is a distributed, self-healing storage layer decoupled from compute — faster failover, faster promotion, auto-scaling storage.
Backups and snapshots are a third, separate mechanism for a third failure mode: data corruption or human error, not instance/AZ loss.
DynamoDB and ElastiCache aren't "smaller RDS" — reach for them for key-based access at scale or hot-read caching, not relational queries.
Match the tool to the exact stated failure domain or access pattern — never assume one mechanism covers all three at once.
